flashcards.back_definition: Verifying who a user or system is before giving access.
flashcards.back_example: Typing a password, then approving a passkey prompt.
flashcards.back_confusion: Authentication proves identity; authorisation decides what that identity may do.
flashcards.back_hook: Who are you? (Then: what may you do?)

flashcards.front: What does a modern password policy include?
flashcards.back_definition: A long minimum length, screening against breached and common passwords, support for long passphrases and paste, rate limiting or lockout, and changes only after suspected compromise.
flashcards.back_example: Rejecting Summer2024! because it appears in breach lists.
flashcards.back_confusion: Mandatory complexity and 90-day rotation are no longer recommended by NIST; they produce predictable passwords.

flashcards.back_definition: People make tiny, predictable changes (Spring2024! to Summer2024!), which attackers guess easily.
flashcards.back_example: A cracked old password lets an attacker predict the new one.
flashcards.back_confusion: Change a password when there is evidence of compromise, not on a timer.

flashcards.front: What is a salt, and what does it defeat?
flashcards.back_definition: A unique random value added to each password before hashing. Identical passwords then have different hashes, which defeats precomputed rainbow tables.
flashcards.back_example: Two users with Password1 get completely different stored hashes.
flashcards.back_confusion: A salt does not slow down guessing one password; a slow hash such as bcrypt or Argon2id does that.

flashcards.front: Why are bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2id used for passwords?
flashcards.back_definition: They are deliberately slow and tunable (work factor, and memory for scrypt and Argon2id), so each guess costs an attacker far more than with a fast hash.
flashcards.back_example: Raising bcrypt's cost by 1 doubles the time per guess.
flashcards.back_confusion: SHA-256 is a fine hash for files but too fast for passwords on its own.
flashcards.back_hook: Slow for you once, slow for them billions of times.

flashcards.front: What did the 2009 RockYou breach teach attackers?
flashcards.back_definition: About 32 million passwords were stored in plain text and leaked, giving a huge list of real human passwords that became a standard cracking wordlist.
flashcards.back_example: rockyou.txt still ships with many penetration testing tools.
flashcards.back_confusion: Every breach of plain or weakly hashed passwords improves attackers' dictionaries.
flashcards.back_hook: Your password may already be in someone's wordlist.

flashcards.front: What are the three MFA factor categories?
flashcards.back_definition: Knowledge (something you know), possession (something you have), inherence (something you are).
flashcards.back_example: Password + hardware key + fingerprint uses all three.
flashcards.back_confusion: A password and a PIN are both knowledge: same category, so not MFA.

flashcards.front: Rank SMS codes, authenticator apps and FIDO2 keys for phishing resistance.
flashcards.back_definition: SMS is weakest (SIM swapping, interception), app codes are better but can still be phished in real time, and FIDO2/WebAuthn keys are phishing-resistant because they are bound to the real domain.
flashcards.back_example: A fake login page can relay an app code, but a security key refuses to sign for the wrong domain.
flashcards.back_confusion: Any MFA is much better than none; the question is how well it resists phishing.

flashcards.back_definition: Flooding a user with push approval prompts until they approve one to make them stop.
flashcards.back_example: Uber's 2022 breach involved repeated push prompts and a message pretending to be IT support.
flashcards.back_confusion: Number matching and showing login location help users spot prompts they didn't start.
flashcards.back_hook: Never approve a prompt you didn't trigger.

flashcards.back_definition: Hijacking steals a valid session token after login and reuses it. Fixation plants a session ID the attacker knows before the victim logs in, then uses it once the victim authenticates.
flashcards.back_example: Fixation: a link carrying ?sessionid=abc123 that the site keeps after login.
flashcards.back_confusion: Regenerating the session ID at login stops fixation; secure cookie flags and HTTPS stop hijacking.
flashcards.back_hook: Fixation plants the key; hijacking pickpockets it.

flashcards.front: What do the Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite cookie flags do?
flashcards.back_definition: Secure: send only over HTTPS. HttpOnly: hide the cookie from JavaScript, which blunts theft through XSS. SameSite: limit sending on cross-site requests, which reduces CSRF.
flashcards.back_confusion: HTTPS alone doesn't stop an XSS script reading a cookie without HttpOnly.
flashcards.back_hook: Secure = tunnel only, HttpOnly = no scripts, SameSite = home only.

flashcards.back_definition: An idle timeout ends a session after a period of no activity. An absolute timeout ends it after a fixed total time, however active the user is.
flashcards.back_example: 15 minutes idle or 8 hours total, whichever comes first.
flashcards.back_confusion: Logging out must also invalidate the session on the server, not just delete the browser cookie.
flashcards.back_hook: Fall asleep or run out the clock.

flashcards.front: DAC, MAC, RBAC and ABAC: what decides access in each?
flashcards.back_definition: DAC: the owner of the resource. MAC: central labels and clearances. RBAC: the user's role. ABAC: attributes of the user, resource and environment, checked at request time.
flashcards.back_example: ABAC: nurses may read records for their own ward during their shift.
flashcards.back_confusion: RBAC asks what role you have; ABAC asks whether the current conditions satisfy the policy.

flashcards.front: Least privilege, separation of duties and just-in-time access?
flashcards.back_definition: Least privilege: only the access needed. Separation of duties: no single person controls a sensitive process end to end. Just-in-time: elevated access granted only for the time it is needed.
flashcards.back_example: One person raises a payment, another approves it; an admin gets domain rights for a 2-hour change window.
flashcards.back_confusion: Malware inherits the rights of whoever runs it, so over-privileged accounts turn one infection into a wide breach.
flashcards.back_hook: Need it, split it, time it.
